summary:
British Columbia stands under the Canadian framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation and hate-propaganda provisions of the Criminal Code, both carried by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms applies in British Columbia, and courts have applied these protections consistently. Sexual orientation has been a protected ground federally since 1996. No province or territory restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, and entry into Canada carries no trans-specific friction for visitors.

British Columbia has no hostile provincial legislation addressing trans people. It was the first jurisdiction in Canada to write sexual orientation into its human-rights code, in 1992, and is routinely assessed as the country's most progressive province on LGBT issues. A 2021 Criminal Code amendment, in force since 2022, made Canada the first country in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults; that ban applies in British Columbia.

Legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration. Transgender people may change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules, and federally issued identity documents can carry an X marker. Provincial human rights machinery is available to visitors and residents who face discrimination in the province.

National hate-crime data shows a mixed picture. A Statistics Canada release of 30 March 2026 covering police-reported hate crime in 2024 records 4,882 incidents, up 1% from 2023 after a 34% rise between 2022 and 2023, and a 169% increase since 2018, with the population rate down 2% to 11.9 per 100,000. Incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, while religion-motivated incidents were essentially stable at 1,342. The release breaks out sexual orientation as a motivation category rather than gender identity, and it contains no British Columbia breakdown, so trans-specific hate-crime volume in the province is not established by this dataset.

Conditions inside correctional institutions are the weakest point in the record. Federal policy is that transgender prisoners are to be placed in correctional facilities according to their gender identity, and transgender prisoners held for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery. Litigation has tested both placement and care: lawyer Barbara findlay represented the transgender prisoner Synthia Kavanagh in a case over gender-affirming medical treatment and placement in a women's institution. A 2022 report alleged that gender-diverse prisoners face a pattern of abuse and discrimination in Canadian jails and are more likely to be victims of sexual assault, while a 2022 study of Nova Scotia correctional officers found them generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety and security, with some concerns about risk to other prisoners. These concerns bear on a trans visitor only if the visitor is detained.
tangentialFactors:
The national baseline score of 0.86 for Canada rests on Charter equality protection, nationwide conversion-therapy criminalisation and legal gender change in every province including British Columbia. It is a comparative index rather than a measure of conditions in the province itself.

Sub-provincial policy turbulence is concentrated elsewhere in the country and primarily affects minors and residents rather than visitors. Saskatchewan's 2023 Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act invoked the notwithstanding clause to require parental consent for students under 16 who ask to use a gender-related preferred name or their gender identity at school; human rights groups called for repeal and litigation followed. Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, the Education Amendment Act and the Fairness and Safety in Sport Act in 2024, then shielded them from legal challenge through Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025, again using the notwithstanding clause. No comparable measure is recorded for British Columbia.

Egale Canada has published a report analysing 2024 police-reported hate-crime incidents affecting 2SLGBTQI people in Canada, offering a sectoral reading of the same national dataset.

Vancouver's Davie Village remains the established social centre for LGBT life in the province.
localsOnly:
British Columbia's human-rights code has covered sexual orientation since 1992, giving residents an explicit provincial basis for discrimination complaints alongside the federal protections in the Canadian Human Rights Act.

Residents are covered by the nationwide conversion-therapy ban that took effect through a 2021 Criminal Code amendment in force since 2022, and by the Criminal Code hate-propaganda and hate-motivation provisions protecting gender identity and gender expression.

Provincial and federal authorities operating correctional institutions in the province are bound by the federal placement policy requiring that transgender prisoners be held according to their gender identity, and by the rule that prisoners held more than 12 continuous months be considered for sex-reassignment surgery.

Parents and students in the province are not subject to the parental-consent and sport-participation regimes adopted in Saskatchewan and Alberta; those measures operate under their own provincial statutes.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Statistics Canada hate-crime figures are national. No British Columbia breakdown is available in the source, so the province's own incident volume and trend remain unresolved.

The Statistics Canada release categories motivation by sexual orientation and not by gender identity. Trans-specific hate-crime volume, in British Columbia or nationally, is not established by this dataset and is unresolved here.

The specific British Columbia procedure and documentary requirements for changing a gender marker on provincial identity documents are not sourced in this inventory; the national framework records only that most provinces permit the change by declaration under varying rules.

Findings from Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis are cited as a source but no specific figures or conclusions from the report are available here, so its content is unresolved.

The corrections evidence cited is national and, in one instance, drawn from Nova Scotia. Conditions in British Columbia's own provincial correctional institutions are not sourced in this inventory.

No source in this inventory addresses hospital or shelter placement policy, airport screening, or visa handling for trans travellers to British Columbia beyond the general finding that entry carries no trans-specific friction.
